Canada Disability Benefit 2026–27: the CAD 204.20 maximum, the working-income exemption and the income test

A worked guide to the federal Canada Disability Benefit for July 2026 to June 2027: the regulation formula, the indexed CAD 204.20 monthly maximum and CAD 10,210 and 14,294 working-income exemptions, the derived income thresholds, why earnings and other income are treated differently, the third-Thursday payment calendar and what a couple’s combined income does. Five charts and an editable model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 9 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original illustration of the federal Canada Disability Benefit (CDB) allocation for the payment period July 2026 to June 2027, based on 2025 adjusted family net income (line 23600 for you and any cohabiting spouse or partner, less RDSP and UCCB income). It applies section 6 of the Canada Disability Benefit Regulations: CAD 2,400, the CAD 10,000 or 14,000 working-income exemption and the CAD 23,000 or 32,500 threshold are each multiplied by the indexing factor you enter (default 1.021); the income above the threshold is reduced at 20%, or 10% for each spouse when both are beneficiaries; the monthly amount is rounded to the cent and an amount of CAD 20 or less a month is paid as one lump sum. ESDC publishes the 2026–27 maximum (CAD 204.20 a month) and exemptions (CAD 10,210 and 14,294) but not the indexed thresholds, so the thresholds here are derived. Eligibility (age 18–64, an approved Disability Tax Credit, filed 2025 returns, residence and status) is assumed. The one-time CAD 150 supplemental amount, provincial or territorial benefits, mid-year changes in marital status and retroactive payments are not modelled.

The central idea

For July 2026 to June 2027 the benefit pays up to CAD 204.20 a month, based on 2025 adjusted family net income. Up to CAD 10,210 of working income (CAD 14,294 for a couple) is ignored; income above an indexed threshold then reduces the benefit by 20 cents per dollar, or 10 cents for each spouse when both receive it. A dollar of wages inside the exemption costs nothing; a dollar of CPP disability or pension income above the threshold costs 20 cents.

01

What the benefit is and who can receive it

The Canada Disability Benefit (CDB) is a federal monthly payment for working-age people with disabilities and low incomes, administered by Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC). The first payments were made in July 2025. It is tax-free: ESDC says payments are not reported as income and no tax slip is issued.

To be eligible a person must, among other conditions:

  • be 18 to 64 years old (eligibility continues in the month of the 65th birthday under the September 2026 amendments);
  • have an approved Disability Tax Credit (DTC) certificate;
  • be a Canadian resident for income tax purposes and a citizen, permanent resident, person registered or entitled to be registered under the Indian Act, protected person, or a temporary resident who has lived in Canada for the previous 18 months;
  • have filed the previous year’s federal return, and have a cohabiting spouse or common-law partner who has also filed. For July 2026 to June 2027 that is the 2025 return.

The benefit is applied for, not automatic, and new recipients are paid from the month after approval. Retroactive payments can reach back up to 24 months before the application was received, but not before June 2025.

02

The formula in the regulations

ESDC’s pages describe the calculation in steps; the underlying rule is section 6 of the Canada Disability Benefit Regulations. The monthly allocation is

(CAD 2,400 × A − reduction) ÷ 12, rounded to the nearest cent,

where A is the indexing factor and the annual reduction is:

Income reduction by household type (section 6 of SOR/2025-35, as amended)
HouseholdIncome testedExempt working incomeThresholdRate
Single, separated, divorced or widowed, or granted a spousal filing waiverYour adjusted incomeLesser of your working income and CAD 10,000 × ACAD 23,000 × A20%
Couple, spouse or partner not a beneficiaryCouple’s combined adjusted incomeLesser of combined working income and CAD 14,000 × ACAD 32,500 × A20%
Couple, both beneficiariesCouple’s combined adjusted incomeLesser of combined working income and CAD 14,000 × ACAD 32,500 × A10% for each spouse

Adjusted income has the Income Tax Act meaning used for the Canada child benefit: line 23600 net income for you and any cohabiting spouse, minus Universal Child Care Benefit and RDSP income (lines 11700 and 12500), plus any of those amounts repaid. Working income is income from employment, self-employment and taxable scholarships. CPP disability benefits, pensions, RRSP withdrawals and investment income count in adjusted income but are not working income.

If the monthly result is CAD 20 or less, the whole year is paid as one lump sum.

03

The 2026–27 amounts: what ESDC publishes and what is derived

All dollar amounts in the formula are 2024 values, multiplied each July by A, the highest annual-average all-items CPI since 2024 divided by the 2024 CPI. July 2026 was the first adjustment.

CDB amounts by payment period
AmountJuly 2025–June 2026July 2026–June 2027Status of the 2026–27 figure
Maximum monthly benefitCAD 200.00CAD 204.20Published by ESDC
Maximum annual benefitCAD 2,400.00CAD 2,450.4012 × the published monthly amount
Working-income exemption, singleCAD 10,000CAD 10,210Published by ESDC
Working-income exemption, coupleCAD 14,000CAD 14,294Published by ESDC
Income threshold, singleCAD 23,000CAD 23,483Derived: 23,000 × 1.021
Income threshold, coupleCAD 32,500CAD 33,182.50Derived: 32,500 × 1.021

Every published 2026–27 figure is exactly 1.021 times its 2024 value, which matches Statistics Canada’s rounded 2.1% annual-average CPI increase for 2025. The unrounded index levels, 164.2 for 2025 and 160.9 for 2024, give 1.02051 instead, which would mean CAD 204.10 a month and a CAD 10,205 exemption. This guide uses 1.021 because it reproduces what ESDC publishes. The model lets you change the factor. Treat the derived thresholds as estimates until ESDC publishes them; its online estimator and examples were still on 2025–26 figures when this guide was reviewed.

04

Worked examples: ESDC’s four cases, then and now

ESDC illustrates the calculation with four households on 2025–26 amounts. The model reproduces each one with the factor set to 1.000, and the right-hand column applies the 2026–27 amounts to the same incomes:

ESDC examples recalculated (monthly benefit per beneficiary)
HouseholdIncome2025–26 (ESDC)2026–27 (this guide)
Jane, singleCAD 16,000, no working incomeCAD 200.00CAD 204.20
Dan, singleCAD 35,000, all employmentCAD 166.67CAD 182.42
Sam, partner Rupinder not eligibleCAD 45,000, all Rupinder’s employmentCAD 200.00CAD 204.20
Donna and Lucia, both eligibleCAD 45,000, CAD 5,000 of it working incomeCAD 137.50 eachCAD 147.39 each

For Dan in 2026–27: CAD 35,000 − 10,210 exempt − 23,483 threshold = CAD 1,307; 20% of that is a CAD 261.40 annual reduction; (CAD 2,450.40 − 261.40) ÷ 12 = CAD 182.42. Indexing helps him by more than CAD 4.20 a month because the exemption and threshold rose too.

The model’s default is a single person with CAD 36,000 of 2025 income: CAD 8,000 from a part-time job and CAD 28,000 from other sources such as a CPP disability benefit. All CAD 8,000 of earnings is exempt, so CAD 36,000 − 8,000 − 23,483 = CAD 4,517 is above the threshold. The reduction is CAD 903.40 a year and the benefit is (2,450.40 − 903.40) ÷ 12 = CAD 128.92 a month, or CAD 1,547.04 for the year.

  • If 2025 earnings had been CAD 3,000 higher, CAD 2,210 of the extra would still fall inside the CAD 10,210 exemption. The benefit would be CAD 115.75 a month, CAD 158.04 less for the year, or 5.3 cents per extra dollar.
  • If the same CAD 3,000 had come from other income, all of it would be tested. The benefit would be CAD 78.92 a month, CAD 600 less for the year, or the full 20 cents per dollar.

Income lower by CAD 4,517 would restore the full CAD 204.20. Above about CAD 43,735 of income, the benefit for this person would be zero.

05

When the money arrives

  • Monthly, on the third Thursday. The Government of Canada calendar lists 16 July, 20 August, 17 September, 15 October, 19 November and 17 December 2026. The same rule gives 21 January, 18 February, 18 March, 15 April, 20 May and 17 June 2027; those dates were not yet published when reviewed.
  • Small amounts are paid at once. If the monthly amount is CAD 20 or less (CAD 240 or less for the year), the whole period is paid as one lump sum on the next payment date.
  • The 2025 return fixes the year. Income earned or withdrawn in 2026 affects the July 2027–June 2028 period, whose amounts have not been published. A reassessment of 2025, or a change in marital status, can change the current amount.
  • A one-time CAD 150 supplemental amount was paid from 17 September 2026 to people who received the benefit between July 2025 and June 2026. People who became eligible from July 2026, or who received a new DTC certificate, are to be paid in a second phase in winter 2027. It is paid automatically for each qualifying DTC certificate.
  • Pausing is final for that period. ESDC says that if you pause or stop payments you cannot later request back payments for that time.

06

Planning points: which income, whose income, which year

  • Earnings are treated more gently than other income. Below the exemption cap a dollar of wages or self-employment income costs no CDB; above it, it costs the same as other income. The extra-income chart shows that difference.
  • RDSP withdrawals are excluded. Disability assistance payments from an RDSP are subtracted in adjusted family net income, so they do not reduce the CDB. RRSP and RRIF withdrawals are fully included, so the calendar year in which they are taken decides which payment period they reduce.
  • A couple is tested together. The couple threshold is higher, but it applies to combined income, so a partner’s raise can reduce the benefit. If both spouses are beneficiaries, each benefit falls by 10 cents per dollar, and the household still loses 20 cents. A spouse granted a filing waiver (for example a partner not resident in Canada, or a separation for reasons the person cannot control) is calculated as single since the September 2026 amendments.
  • Count the whole stack. In the phase-out range the CDB’s 20% sits on top of income tax, payroll contributions and other income-tested benefits such as the Canada workers benefit and its disability supplement, the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit and provincial programs. Provinces and territories set their own treatment of the CDB in social assistance; check your program before counting the benefit as extra cash.
  • File every year, on time. Both spouses’ returns are a condition of eligibility, even with no income.

07

What the official figures show

In its release of 10 September 2026, ESDC reported that 335,650 people had received Canada Disability Benefit payments totalling CAD 813,074,098 since July 2025. These are cumulative counts of people ever paid and dollars paid “to date”. They are not the number of current monthly recipients, and the release gives no as-of date.

Dividing one by the other gives about CAD 2,422 per person ever paid. That figure mixes people paid for different numbers of months, partial benefits and retroactive lump sums, so it is not an average monthly or annual entitlement. ESDC has not published a breakdown by household type or income in the sources reviewed.

08

Limits of the model

The model applies the regulation formula to one household for the whole payment period, using the indexing factor entered and the published or derived amounts above. It assumes the eligibility conditions are met and leaves out the CAD 150 supplemental amount, retroactive and first-payment catch-up amounts, mid-year changes in marital status, incarceration rules, debts set off against payments and every provincial or territorial program. Working income is entered as one combined figure for a couple. Annual amounts are twelve rounded monthly payments. Check your benefit in your My Service Canada Account or with ESDC for your actual entitlement.

Federal benefit only; no personal entitlement estimate. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.
